title: Unions and Advocacy Groups Sue to Block Trump's Fixed-Term Visa Rule
excerpt: A federal lawsuit filed in Massachusetts challenges the 'duration of status' rule change that would cap F, J, and I visa stays at four years — affecting hundreds of thousands of students and exchange visitors.
body:
• Unions and advocacy groups filed suit in the District of Massachusetts on August 18 to block a new rule that would cap F, J, and I visa stays at a fixed four-year term
  • The rule, set to take effect September 15, eliminates the longstanding 'duration of status' framework that allowed visa holders to stay as long as their program lasted
  • Indian nationals are the largest group of F-1 visa holders in the US, meaning the rule change disproportionately impacts the Indian student community
  • Plaintiffs argue the rule change would create mass uncertainty, with visa holders potentially losing status mid-degree or mid-training

The Lawsuit

A coalition of labor unions and immigration advocacy groups filed a federal lawsuit on Monday in the District of Massachusetts seeking to block a Trump administration rule that would fundamentally change how long foreign students and exchange visitors can remain in the United States.

https://x.com/washingtonpost/status/2089766816151138702

The rule, scheduled to take effect on September 15, would eliminate the longstanding "duration of status" framework for F-1 student visas, J-1 exchange visitor visas, and I visas for foreign media representatives. Under the current system, these visa holders are admitted for the duration of their program — meaning a student can stay as long as they are enrolled and in good standing. The new rule would replace that with a fixed maximum stay of four years.

The plaintiffs argue the change would throw hundreds of thousands of people into legal limbo. Students midway through doctoral programs, researchers on multi-year fellowships, and journalists on extended assignments could find themselves out of status with no recourse — forced to either leave the country or file costly extensions with an immigration system already overwhelmed by backlogs.

"This rule would upend the lives of hundreds of thousands of students and exchange visitors who came to the United States following the rules as they existed."

— Plaintiff filing, D. Mass.

Why It Matters for Indian Nationals

Indian nationals represent the largest group of F-1 visa holders in the United States, a position they have held for several years running. In the 2024-25 academic year, over 330,000 Indian students were enrolled at American universities, many in STEM programs that routinely take five to seven years to complete — well beyond the proposed four-year cap.

The impact extends beyond students. The J-1 visa is widely used by Indian researchers, physicians in residency programs, and professionals participating in training programs at American companies and universities. A fixed-term cap would create a new cliff for each of these groups, forcing periodic re-applications in a system where processing times already stretch to months.

For NRI families with children studying in the US, the rule introduces a layer of uncertainty that could reshape college planning. Parents weighing the cost and commitment of an American education now face the prospect of their child's legal status expiring before their degree is complete.

The Administration's Position

The Trump administration has framed the rule change as a matter of immigration enforcement and national security. Officials have argued that the open-ended duration of status framework makes it difficult to track visa overstays and creates opportunities for abuse. By imposing fixed terms, the administration says it can better monitor who is in the country and for how long.

Critics counter that the existing system already has robust tracking mechanisms through the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, known as SEVIS, which requires schools to report on the enrollment status of international students. The Government Accountability Office has not identified duration of status as a significant source of visa overstays in its recent reports.

What Happens Next

The lawsuit seeks a preliminary injunction to block the rule before its September 15 effective date. Given the compressed timeline, a ruling could come within weeks. Similar challenges to immigration rule changes have had mixed success in federal courts, with outcomes often hinging on whether the administration followed proper notice-and-comment procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act.

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian students and professionals currently in the US on F and J visas, the coming weeks will be a period of anxious waiting. The outcome of this lawsuit could determine whether they can finish what they started — or face a sudden and forced departure from the country they chose to study and work in.
